## 1. What you'll build, and why

`struct` gave you *product* types — "all of these fields at once." `enum` gives you *sum* types —
"exactly **one** of these **cases**." Together they're **algebraic data types** (ADTs), and they're
how you model data that comes in alternatives: a result that's success *or* failure, a shape that's a
circle *or* a rectangle, a value that's present *or* `nil` (that last one is `Optional`, concept 13 —
it's an enum). You'll add `enum` through the whole compiler, represented the way every compiler
represents a sum type: a **tagged union**.

- **You implement:** enum *construction* in SILGen and the enum LLVM instructions in IRGen.
- **Outcome:** enum programs **run and match swiftc** — case equality, raw values, enums in
  conditionals.
- **Out of scope (by design):** taking an enum *apart* — reading a case's associated values — needs
  `switch`, which is **concept 12**. That's why enums and pattern matching are a pair.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### A sum type is a tag plus a payload

A value of `enum Shape { case circle(Int); case rect(Int, Int); case dot }` is exactly one case at a
time. You can't store both a circle and a rectangle, so you don't need room for both — you need a
**tag** saying which case it is, and enough **payload** for the *widest* case's associated values:

![A tagged union: every `Shape` value is the same size — a tag (which case) plus a payload sized to the widest case. `circle(5)` is `{tag 0, 5, –}`, `rect(3,4)` is `{tag 1, 3, 4}`, `dot` is `{tag 2, –, –}`.](figs/tagged_union.png)

We lay this out as an LLVM aggregate `%Shape = type { i64, i64, i64 }` — field 0 is the tag, fields
1… are the payload slots (sized to the widest case; unused slots are just dead for narrower cases).
This is the naive-but-honest layout; real swiftc is far cleverer (it packs the tag into **spare
bits** of the payload when it can — see `swift/lib/IRGen/GenEnum.cpp`), but the *idea* is identical.

### Construction: pick a tag, fill the payload

`Color.red` and `Shape.circle(5)` both lower to one SIL instruction, **`enum #tag (payload…)`**, which
builds the aggregate: store the case's **index** as the tag, then the associated values into the
payload slots. `Color.red` → `enum #0 ()`; `Shape.rect(3, 4)` → `enum #1 (%a, %b)`. In LLVM that's an
`insertvalue` chain, exactly like a struct — the tag is just field 0.

### Raw values and equality — what you *can* do without `switch`

Without pattern matching you still have two useful operations, and both reduce to **reading the tag**
(`enum_tag`, an `extractvalue 0`):

- **`.rawValue`** on a `: Int` raw-value enum is the case's raw integer. With Swift's implicit raws
  (`north = 0, south = 1, …`) the raw value *is* the tag, so `Dir.south.rawValue` is just the tag, `1`.
- **`==`** on a payload-free enum compares the tags: `Color.green == Color.green` is `tag == tag`.

There's a real parity subtlety here, and we match swiftc on both sides of it: a payload-free enum is
**implicitly `Equatable`**, so `==` just works; but an **associated-value** enum's `==` has to compare
payloads *per case*, which Swift only synthesizes when you declare `: Equatable` (with all payloads
Equatable). Without that conformance, swiftc **rejects** `Shape.circle(5) == …` — and so do we
("type 'Shape' does not conform to protocol 'Equatable'"). Tag-only equality would be *wrong*
(`circle(5)` would equal `circle(6)`), so refusing it is the correct, faithful behaviour.

### Why you can't read a payload yet

You can build `Shape.circle(5)` and compare tags, but you can't ask "what's the radius?" — that means
"*if* this is a `circle`, bind its `Int`," which is a **pattern**. Reading associated values safely
requires checking the tag first (you mustn't read `rect`'s second field out of a `circle`), and that
tag-check-then-extract is exactly what `switch` compiles to. So associated-value enums are *built*
here and *used* in concept 12 — the two halves of ADTs.

### The subset you are growing into

**New lexemes.** Two keywords, both in `token.ml`'s `keyword_or_ident` table; nothing new in the
scanner itself, since `.` and `;` arrived with concept 10:

| spelling | token | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `enum` | `Token.Kw_enum` | a keyword — starts a top-level item, like `struct` and `func` |
| `case` | `Token.Kw_case` | a keyword, legal only inside an `enum` body (concept 12 gives it a second home, inside `switch`) |

**The grammar** — `<-- new` marks what this concept adds; everything else is concepts 05–10.
Notation is EBNF: `[ x ]` is *optional* (zero or one), `{ x }` is *repetition* (zero or more),
`|` separates alternatives, and quoted text is a terminal.

```
program     ::= [ nl ] [ item { nl item } ] [ nl ]
nl          ::= NEWLINE { NEWLINE }     # a run of blank lines is one separator
item        ::= enum_decl                                          <-- new
              | struct_decl
              | func_decl
              | statement
enum_decl   ::= "enum" ident [ ":" ident ] "{"                     <-- new (the `: Int` raw type)
                  [ nl ] [ case_line { nl case_line } ] [ nl ] "}"
case_line   ::= "case" case { "," case }                           <-- new (several per line)
case        ::= ident [ "(" ident { "," ident } ")" ]              <-- new (associated values)

statement   ::= ("let" | "var") ident [ ":" type ] "=" expr
              | ident "=" expr
              | ident "." ident "=" expr
              | "if" expr block [ "else" ( block | if-statement ) ]
              | "while" expr block
              | "for" ident "in" expr "..<" expr block
              | "break" | "continue" | "return" [ expr ]
              | expr
type        ::= "Int" | "Double" | "Bool" | "String" | "Void"
              | ident                                                (a struct OR an enum name)

expr        ::= or
or          ::= and { "||" and }                                     (bp 3)
and         ::= comparison { "&&" comparison }                       (bp 4)
comparison  ::= cast { ("==" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">=") cast } (bp 5)
cast        ::= sum { "as" type }                                    (bp 7)
sum         ::= product { ("+" | "-") product }                      (bp 10)
product     ::= unary { ("*" | "/" | "%") unary }                    (bp 20)
unary       ::= "-" unary | postfix
postfix     ::= primary { "." ident [ "(" [ arg { "," arg } ] ")" ] }  <-- the call form is new
primary     ::= int | float | string | "true" | "false" | ident
              | ident "(" [ arg { "," arg } ] ")"
              | "(" expr ")"
arg         ::= [ ident ":" ] expr
```

Three things to notice. The enum body is **not** a list of statements: `parse_enum` has its own
loop, and one `case` line may declare several cases (`case red, green, blue`) — they are numbered
left to right, which is the ordering the raw-value tests pin. An **associated-value list is a list
of types**, not of parameters: `circle(Int)` has no argument label, which is why `Shape.circle(5)`
is a positional call. And the postfix production grew a **call form**, so `E.case(1, 2)` parses as
one node (`Ast.Method_call`) rather than as a member access applied to a call: `.` followed by an
identifier followed by `(` is a case construction here, and the same shape becomes method calls in
Phase 5. Nothing in the *expression* grammar knows about enums — sema decides, from the registry,
whether `Color.red` names a case or is a member access on a value.

### The new SIL instructions (swiftc's shape)

| SIL | meaning | LLVM |
|---|---|---|
| `enum #t (payload…)` | build a value of case `t` | `insertvalue` (tag at #0, payload at #1…) |
| `enum_tag %e` | read the case tag (an `Int`) | `extractvalue %e, 0` |

swiftc's real instructions are `enum`/`unchecked_enum_data`/`select_enum`; `enum_tag` stands in for
"read the discriminator." Concept 12 will add the destructuring counterpart.

### The diagnostics sema owes you (given)

You write no diagnostics in this concept — sema is given — but the lowering may assume every rule
below has already fired, and `sema-enums.t` keeps them on record. Wording follows `swiftc
-typecheck` where the subset lets it (`swift/include/swift/AST/DiagnosticsSema.def`, line numbers
from the pinned snapshot); the differences are stated, not hidden.

| program | our message | swiftc |
|---|---|---|
| `Color.blue`, no such case | `type 'Color' has no member 'blue'` | **same** (`could_not_find_type_member`, l.86) — note "type", not "value of type": the receiver is the enum *type* |
| `Color.red.rawValue` on a plain enum | `value of type 'Color' has no member 'rawValue'` | **same** (`could_not_find_value_member`, l.70) — `rawValue` exists only under a `: Int` raw type |
| `S.pair(1)` for `case pair(Int, Int)` | `enum case 'S.pair' expects 2 associated value(s) but 1 given` | `missing argument for parameter #2 in call` (`missing_argument_positional`, l.1686) — one message per missing value; ours reports the arity once |
| `S.pair(1, true)` | `cannot convert value of type 'Bool' to specified type 'Int'` | `… to expected argument type 'Int'` (`cannot_convert_argument_value`, l.382) — we reuse 05's `check_expr` wording |
| `S.a(1) == S.a(1)` | `type 'S' does not conform to protocol 'Equatable'` (`type_does_not_conform`, l.2897 — a real swiftc line, at a different site) | `referencing operator function '==' on 'Equatable' requires that 'S' conform to 'Equatable'` (`type_does_not_conform_in_decl_ref`, l.2984) — same verdict, longer sentence |
| `C.a == C.b`, payload-free | **accepted** | **accepted** — a payload-free enum is implicitly `Equatable` |
| `enum A {…}` and `struct A {…}` | `invalid redeclaration of 'A'` | **same** (`invalid_redecl`, l.1110) — one namespace for both kinds |
| `let n: Int = Color.red` | `cannot convert value of type 'Color' to specified type 'Int'` | **same** |
| `let e = E.a` where `case a(Int)` | `enum case 'E.a' requires arguments` | **accepted** — swiftc reads a bare payload case as its *constructor function*, `(Int) -> E`. Our subset has no function values until concept 29, so we refuse instead of inferring a type we cannot represent |
| `print(c)` of an enum | `cannot print a value of type 'Color' (only Int, Double, Bool and String)` | **accepted** — swiftc prints `red` through reflection; ours has no runtime to do it, so sema refuses rather than letting IRGen crash |

The struct rules of concept 10 are still live and still checked here — the memberwise
initializer's labels, `p.x = e` needing a `var` binding and a `var` field, `==` on two structs.

## 3. Build it, step by step

The front end is given — the parser builds the declarations, sema fills the enum registry and has
already rejected everything in the table above. Three holes, in this order:

- **`silgen.ml`, `TODO(11)` in `gen_expr`, the `Member (Var tn, case, _)` arm** — `Color.red`,
  a case with no associated values. It must become **one** `Sil.Enum` instruction whose tag is the
  case's index in the declaration and whose payload list is empty, typed `Types.TEnum tn`. The
  layout is `Hashtbl.find b.enums tn`; `Types.case_index` turns the case *name* into that index.
  `silgen-case.t` prints the SIL and pins the tag.
- **`silgen.ml`, `TODO(11)` in the `Method_call (Var tn, case, args, _)` arm** — `Shape.rect(3, 4)`.
  The same instruction, with the arguments **evaluated first** (left to right, each through
  `gen_expr`) and handed over as the payload. `silgen-payload.t` pins both the operand order and
  the tag, which counts every case, payload-carrying or not.
- **`irgen.ml`, `TODO(11)`** — the two instructions in LLVM. `Enum` builds the aggregate the way
  `Struct` does in concept 10, an `insertvalue` chain from `undef`, except that field 0 is the
  **tag** (an `i64` constant, not an operand) and the payload starts at field 1. `Enum_tag` reads
  field 0 back out. `llty (vty v)` gives the LLVM type of a value, `fresh ()` a register, `opnd` the
  operand of a SIL value.

Reference: `solution/` — after you have tried it.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase3-value-types/11-enums-adts
```

Every `.t` file calls `./lab.exe`, built from **this directory's** library, so the report is about
your code here. In the order you fill the holes:

- `sema-enums.t` — `--typecheck`: the given rules from the table above, green from the start. It
  is the contract the lowering may rely on (no unknown case, no payload mismatch, no `==` on an
  associated-value enum ever reaches SILGen).
- `silgen-case.t` — `--emit-sil`: `Color.green` is `enum #1 () $Color`; the tag follows the
  declaration order whether the cases are written on one line or several; `==` is two `enum_tag`
  reads and an integer compare; `.rawValue` is the same `enum_tag`; an enum in a `var`, and one
  crossing a function boundary. No program here carries a payload, so this file goes green with
  the first hole alone.
- `silgen-payload.t` — `--emit-sil`: `Shape.rect(3, 4)` is `enum #1 (%0, %1)`, with the payload
  evaluated before the case is built; a one-value case; an arbitrary expression as an associated
  value; a tag that counts payload-free cases too; a call result as a payload. No program here
  builds a payload-free case, so this file goes green with the second hole alone.
- `irgen-enums.t` — `--emit-llvm` then `build`: the one-field aggregate of a payload-free enum,
  the widest-case sizing, the `insertvalue` chain with the tag at 0, `extractvalue … , 0`; then
  programs **run** — tag equality, the raw values 0/1/3, the left-to-right case order, an enum
  driving a loop, an enum through a function, and an associated-value enum built and passed on.
- `test_enums.ml` (alcotest `enums`) — the same four groups in-process: `sema-enums` (given — its
  three cases pass on the skeleton), `silgen-case`, `silgen-payload`, `irgen-enums`.
- `oracle.t` — **the headline**, in two halves. The runtime half compiles the 16 programs of
  `oracle-corpus.txt` with `swiftc -Onone` and with `./lab.exe build`, runs both binaries, and
  demands identical stdout and exit code; when ours refuses with a `TODO(` the loop stops, so it
  stays red until the last hole is filled. The front-end half asks `swiftc -typecheck` and
  `./lab.exe --typecheck` for a verdict on the 18 programs of `typecheck-corpus.txt` — six
  well-formed, twelve the enum rules must refuse — and they must agree; that half needs no
  lowering, so it is green from the start.

A hole you have not started shows as `TODO` with the list of what it will check; a hole in
progress shows `FAIL` with, under each failing case, what the test wants and what your code
printed. On the untouched skeleton the two silgen files and `irgen-enums.t` are `TODO`,
`sema-enums.t` is `PASS`, `oracle.t` is `FAIL` with its front-end half already `OK`, and the
alcotest is `FAIL` with its three sema cases `OK`.

## 5. Benchmark it

An enum is the size of its widest case (plus tag), regardless of which case is live — so a
`{ huge payload | empty case }` enum wastes space in the empty case. swiftc's spare-bit packing
reclaims much of this; `Optional` (concept 13) is the famous win (`Optional<SomePointer>` is the same
size as the pointer, using an invalid bit pattern as the `nil` tag). Ours is unpacked — the honest
baseline a Phase-4/layout pass would later optimize.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Explicit raw values.** Support `case north = 1` (and `enum E: String`): store the per-case raw in
   the layout and lower `.rawValue` to that constant (a small tag→raw map) instead of the tag.
2. **`Equatable` for associated values.** When the enum declares `: Equatable`, synthesize `==`: compare
   tags, and *if equal*, `switch` on the tag and compare the live payload slots. (Needs concept 12's
   switch — circle back after it.)
3. **Indirect (recursive) enums.** `indirect enum Expr { case lit(Int); case add(Expr, Expr) }`. A
   recursive case can't be inline (infinite size), so its payload is **boxed** (a pointer). Add an
   `indirect` flag and lower the payload to a heap pointer — the seed of the ADT interpreter that is
   Milestone M3.

## 7. Recap & what's next

You added `enum` — the **sum** half of algebraic data types — as a **tagged union**: a tag plus a
payload sized to the widest case. Construction picks a tag and fills the payload; `.rawValue` and `==`
read the tag. Enum programs run and match swiftc.

Next, **12-pattern-matching**: `switch`. It's the missing half — it reads the **tag**, branches to the
matching `case`, and **binds the associated values** (`case .circle(let r):`), with **exhaustiveness**
checking so you can't forget a case. That's when `Shape.circle(5)` finally gives up its `5`, and when
the tagged unions you just built become the ADTs that make Swift Swift.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

From `solution/silgen.ml` (construction) and `solution/irgen.ml` (the LLVM):

```ocaml
(* SILGen — an enum case is a tag + payload values *)
| Ast.Member (Ast.Var (tn, _), case, _) when Hashtbl.mem b.enums tn ->
    let el = Hashtbl.find b.enums tn in
    emit b (Sil.Enum (Option.get (Types.case_index el case), [])) (Types.TEnum tn)
| Ast.Method_call (Ast.Var (tn, _), case, args, _) when Hashtbl.mem b.enums tn ->
    let el = Hashtbl.find b.enums tn in
    let argvs = List.map (fun (_, e) -> gen_expr b e) args in
    emit b (Sil.Enum (Option.get (Types.case_index el case), argvs)) (Types.TEnum tn)
```

```ocaml
(* IRGen — a tagged union in LLVM: tag at #0, payload at #1.. *)
| Sil.Enum (tag, payload) ->
    let ety = llty (vty v) in
    let r0 = fresh () in
    p (Printf.sprintf "  %s = insertvalue %s undef, i64 %d, 0\n" r0 ety tag);
    let acc = ref r0 in
    List.iteri (fun idx fv ->
      let r = fresh () in
      p (Printf.sprintf "  %s = insertvalue %s %s, %s %s, %d\n"
           r ety !acc (llty (vty fv)) (op fv) (idx + 1));
      acc := r) payload;
    Hashtbl.replace opnd v !acc
| Sil.Enum_tag a ->
    let r = fresh () in
    p (Printf.sprintf "  %s = extractvalue %s %s, 0\n" r (llty (vty a)) (op a));
    Hashtbl.replace opnd v r
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — explicit raw values

Give `enum_layout` a `raws : int list` (parsed from `= N`, defaulting to the index). Lower `.rawValue`
not to `enum_tag` but to a lookup: in the simplest form, since the tag *is* the case index, emit a
`switch`/`select` over the tag returning the matching `raws` constant. For `enum E: String`, store the
strings as globals and return the pointer.

### 2 — Equatable synthesis

With `: Equatable`, generate `==` as: `enum_tag a == enum_tag b` and, when equal, a `switch` on the tag
where each case compares its live payload slots (`unchecked_enum_data` in real SIL). This is the same
derived-conformance machinery as struct `Equatable`, plus a tag dispatch — and it's exactly what
concept 12's `switch` lowering gives you, so it's a natural follow-on.

### 3 — indirect enums

A recursive enum has unbounded size, so Swift **boxes** the recursive payload: the case stores a
pointer to a heap allocation holding the associated values. Add `indirect` to the case, lower
construction to a `malloc` + store, and lower extraction (in `switch`) to a load through the pointer.
This is what lets `enum Expr { case add(Expr, Expr) }` exist — and a tree-walking evaluator over it,
written in our Swift subset and matching swiftc, is **Milestone M3**.
```
